title: Pâte brisée, French shortcrust
subtitle: The standard French pastry for quiche, savoury tarts, and single-crust pies
excerpt: Pâte brisée is the French equivalent of British shortcrust: flour, cold butter, a little water, and an egg yolk for richness. It is less sweet than pâte sucrée and more buttery and tender than plain British shortcrust. The egg yolk makes it easier to roll and more forgiving in the tin.
sourceNotes: Pâte brisée is a classical French pastry base. The egg-yolk addition and higher butter content compared to British shortcrust are standard features of the French method.

recipe.yieldDescription: Enough for one 23 cm tart or quiche case
recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap the disc tightly and freeze for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge before rolling.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Wrap and freeze one disc for later.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for 2 days before use.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional oven for blind baking; fan 170°C

glossaryTerms.definition: French shortcrust pastry, enriched with egg yolk and a higher proportion of butter than British shortcrust. Used for quiche, savoury tarts, and any single-crust pie where a tender, buttery case is wanted.

content.text: is the standard French pastry for quiche lorraine, savoury tarts, and tourtes. The egg yolk makes it more pliable than plain British shortcrust and the higher butter ratio gives it a richer, more crumbly texture. It is not sweet.

200 g plain flour, 125 g cold unsalted butter, 1 egg yolk, 2 to 3 tbsp cold water, ½ tsp salt. The higher butter ratio (roughly 60% of the flour weight, versus 50% in standard shortcrust) is what gives pâte brisée its richness.
Rub the cold butter into the flour and salt until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs with some pea-sized pieces remaining.
Beat the egg yolk with 2 tbsp cold water. Add to the flour and mix with a palette knife until the dough just comes together. If it is too dry, add the third tablespoon of water.
Press the dough into a disc, wrap, and chill for at least 30 minutes before rolling.

Roll on a lightly floured surface to 3 mm. Pâte brisée is slightly more fragile than British shortcrust because of the higher butter content. If it tears while draping into the tin, press the tear together with wet fingers. Chill the lined tin for 20 minutes before blind baking at 190°C (conventional) for 15 minutes, then a further 8 minutes without the beans.
